name: Usage-based billing / metering / SaaS quotas
category: Adjacent — metering for usage-based billing and tenant quotas
parent_research_topic: Beava use cases — current and potential applications of beava as a real-time feature server

domain_fit.domain_name: Usage-based billing / metering / SaaS-quota infrastructure — per-tenant per-API-key rolling consumption counters with audit-grade durability
domain_fit.one_line_definition: A finance / billing-platform team ingests every billable customer action (API call, LLM token, GB-egress, compute-second, row scanned, agent step) and serves per-(tenant, plan_dimension) rolling counters to (a) a real-time prepaid-credit/quota gate that must decide gate vs allow on the next request in single-digit milliseconds, and (b) a downstream invoice/rating pipeline that requires the same counters be reconcilable to an external auditor 12+ months later.
domain_fit.representative_jobs_to_be_done: 1) Power a real-time prepaid-credit wallet: 'tenant X has 2.3M credits left; this request costs 1.7k input tokens + 0.4k output tokens × model multiplier — debit and decide allow/deny inline before the LLM round-trip', returned in <5 ms so the gate does not add latency to the served product. 2) Enforce contract quotas / plan limits per (api_key_id, route, plan_tier): 'this api_key has consumed 9.7M of its 10M monthly included calls — surface 'usage 97%' header, warn at 50/80/95%, hard-stop at 100%', with the same counter feeding the customer-facing 'current usage' dashboard the finance / customer-success team uses for upsell conversations. 3) Compute multi-dimensional billable usage in real time: sum, count, count-distinct, max-concurrent (for seat / connection pricing), tiered/graduated/volume-bracket rating per (tenant_id, sku, region, currency, billing_period), and expose a 'projected_invoice_amount_so_far' feature that the customer-portal renders at sub-second freshness. 4) Detect billing anomalies and abuse inline: per-tenant velocity (rate-of-change of usage), n_unique downstream calls per minute, geographic / device dispersion of API-key usage — combine with the same counters to revoke a leaked key or freeze a runaway script before the invoice closes. 5) Produce a reconcilable audit trail: every meter event is durably journaled with an idempotency key, and at month-end the billing system can replay or re-aggregate from the event log to certify the invoice against the live counter — the standard 'two-aggregations-must-tie' SOX / SOC1 control.
domain_fit.event_shapes: meter_event {idempotency_key (UUID, required, unique within ≥24 h window — Stripe pattern), tenant_id, customer_id, subscription_id, api_key_id, meter_name (e.g. 'api_calls', 'llm_input_tokens', 'llm_output_tokens', 'gb_egress', 'compute_seconds', 'rows_scanned', 'agent_steps', 'seats_active'), quantity (decimal/int), unit ('tokens'|'requests'|'bytes'|'seconds'|'rows'), occurred_at (event-time, authoritative for billing-period assignment), recorded_at (ingest-time, for arrival monitoring), sku_id / price_id, plan_tier, region, currency, request_id (for join-back), metadata{...} (model_name, cache_hit, route, http_status, agent_id)}. The Stripe Billing Meter Event object, the OpenMeter CloudEvents shape and the Lago event schema are all minor variations of this. Volume is dominated by high-frequency primitives: per-request meter_event for API-as-a-product (one per served HTTP call), per-token-batch for LLM platforms (sub-second cadence), per-second for compute / minutes for storage. Late-arriving events are normal (mobile / edge replay) and must be slotted into the correct billing period by occurred_at, not arrival time.
domain_fit.feature_shapes: Almost exclusively SUM and COUNT primitives over per-(tenant_id, meter_name, billing_period) keys — usage_total_current_period, usage_total_today, usage_total_last_hour, usage_total_last_minute, usage_total_per_route, usage_total_per_model, plus the corresponding *_in_units feature after applying a price function. Auxiliary primitives: n_unique_api_keys_per_tenant_per_day (CMS / HLL acceptable for soft signals only — exact for billing), max_concurrent_seats / max_concurrent_connections (a high-water-mark gauge, sampled and aggregated by max-over-window for seat-style pricing), velocity (rate-of-change of usage for anomaly + runaway-script detection), tiered_bracket_index (current position in a 0–1k / 1k–10k / 10k+ graduated price ladder, computed from usage_total_current_period), projected_invoice_amount (sum of tiered rates × usage per meter), credit_balance_remaining (a decrement-only counter sourced from a separately-loaded prepaid wallet event). Distribution / percentile primitives are not used for billing itself but are useful for the 'noisy-neighbor / abuse' overlay. Windowing is overwhelmingly tumbling (calendar month / day / hour billing periods plus a small set of rolling 1m / 5m / 1h velocity windows for the quota gate); session windows are unused; sliding windows appear only on the quota-enforcement side, not the invoicing side.
domain_fit.entity_grain: Composite, with the dominant key being (tenant_id, meter_name, billing_period_id). Secondary keys are (api_key_id, meter_name, billing_period_id) for per-key fairness / leak detection and (subscription_id, sku_id, billing_period_id) for the invoicing pipeline. Customer_id and tenant_id are often distinct (one customer many tenants/workspaces, especially for multi-product platforms). The api_key_id grain is the dominant cardinality driver — typical SaaS has 1–10 keys per tenant, large platforms have 100s, agentic / per-end-user-key deployments have 1000s+. Billing_period_id is bounded (monthly, with a small overlap window for late events and reopens).
domain_fit.window_semantics_required: Tumbling per calendar billing period (month) is the source-of-truth window — every event has exactly one billing period assigned by occurred_at, and the closed-period count is the invoiced number. Daily / hourly tumbling windows are needed for customer-facing 'today's usage' / 'this hour' surfaces and for prorating mid-cycle plan changes. Sliding rolling windows (1m, 5m, 1h) are needed only on the quota-enforcement / anomaly-detection side. EXACT aggregates are mandatory for any counter that feeds an invoice — HLL / CMS / t-digest are explicitly forbidden on the billing primary because finance auditors will not accept probabilistic dollar amounts. Approximate aggregates are acceptable only for the 'abuse / noisy-neighbor' overlay that runs in parallel. Late-arriving events must be placed in the correct historical period; Lago documents this explicitly and reopens recently-closed periods up to a grace cutoff.
domain_fit.exactly_once_or_idempotency_needs: Strict exactly-once at the counter level — every dollar that lands on the invoice is a dollar a customer can dispute, and double-counting is a regulator-visible defect. The universal pattern is (a) producer assigns a unique idempotency_key per meter_event, (b) the metering system dedups within a window (Stripe enforces ≥24 h, OpenMeter dedups by (id, source) for 32 d by default), (c) the aggregator commits to durable storage exactly-once (Kafka transactional writes + idempotent ClickHouse sink or equivalent), (d) reconciliation jobs replay raw events against the live counter at month-end. This is the single hardest non-functional requirement of this domain and is non-negotiable.

technical_fit.latency_budget: Two distinct regimes. (i) Inline quota / prepaid-credit gate: read p99 <5–10 ms, because the gate is on the request path of the served product (LLM API, search API, etc.) and any added latency directly degrades the product's own SLA — Redis-Lua sliding-window-counter gates publish sub-5 ms p99 today and that is the bar. beava's sub-ms TCP+msgpack get / batch_get sits comfortably under this budget. (ii) Invoicing / dashboard / 'current usage' UI: 100 ms – 1 s tolerated; minutes acceptable for monthly invoice close. The inline-gate budget is what disqualifies most warehouse-flavoured metering stacks (Lago, OpenMeter, Orb all sit on ClickHouse and answer in the 50–500 ms band, which is fine for dashboards but too slow for an inline gate on every LLM call).
technical_fit.feature_freshness_sla: Sub-second freshness is mandatory for the quota gate (the very next request must see the previous request's debit, otherwise concurrent requests overshoot the credit balance — the textbook OCS / online-charging-system problem). 1–5 s freshness is acceptable for the customer-facing 'today's usage' dashboard. Minutes-to-hours is acceptable for invoice computation. OpenMeter explicitly pre-aggregates into 1-minute tumbling windows on the ClickHouse path, which puts them behind the inline-gate freshness regime; that is the architectural gap a feature-server-style metering tier would close.
technical_fit.throughput_profile: Steady-state: 1k – 100k EPS for a typical mid-size SaaS billing platform (one meter event per billable customer action; ratio to product RPS is product-specific — an LLM platform emits 2–4 meter events per chat turn for input/output/cache tokens). Peak: 10x steady-state during launch / promo / outage-recovery replay storms. Reference points: Stripe Billing Meter Event Streams v2 is rate-limited at 10k req/s livemode (contact sales for more); Lago publicly demonstrates 1M EPS sustained on ClickHouse Cloud (post-2024 migration, with one named enterprise customer required to drive that bar); Orb publishes 250k+ EPS; OpenMeter Y-Combinator pitch claims 'millions of events per second' on ClickHouse + Kafka. beava's published ~684k EPS per Apple-M4 core (TCP+msgpack, parallel=16) sits between Orb and Lago's headline number and is competitive on raw EPS — but for billing the constraining factor is not EPS, it is durability + exactly-once, which is where the comparison gets harder. [uncertain]
technical_fit.read_to_write_ratio: Write-heavy on the metering side (one write per billable action, multiple keys updated per event due to fanout into (tenant, meter, period), (api_key, meter, period), (subscription, sku, period) rollups — typically 3–10 key updates per event). Read-balanced-to-heavy on the quota-gate side (every inline gate is a read; if every request goes through the gate the ratio approaches 1:1 with writes). Read-light on the invoicing side (a single batch read per closing). Aggregate over a mature deployment is roughly 1–3 reads per write.
technical_fit.state_size_estimate: Dominated by (tenant_id × meter_name × billing_period_id) cardinality. Typical mid-size SaaS: 1k–100k tenants × 5–30 meters × ~12 open billing periods (current + grace + audit window) = 60k – 36M composite keys; at ~200–500 B per key (a handful of int / decimal sums, an idempotency-dedup ring, a small metadata blob), that is 12 MB – 18 GB hot state — well within a single beava node. The api_key_id grain explodes this 5–500x (1M – 1B composite keys), pushing the hot state into the hundreds-of-GB range for large platforms with agentic / per-end-user keys, which exceeds a single in-memory node and requires hand-sharding. The brutal pathological case is including request_id or event_id in the key for dedup; the only sane pattern is a rolling bloom / set scoped to the idempotency window, not a per-key permanent set. [uncertain]
technical_fit.cardinality_pattern: Mixed. tenant_id grows slowly (1k–1M, signup-rate-bounded). meter_name is bounded (typically 5–30 named meters per product). billing_period_id is bounded (monthly + small window). sku_id / price_id is bounded (10–1000 prices). The explosive dimensions are api_key_id (especially for AI agent platforms where keys are issued per end-user — millions to tens of millions) and per-row metadata (model_name, route — bounded; but cache_hit, prompt_hash, request_id — unbounded and should not be keys, only payload). The 'survive cardinality' positioning of beava maps directly to the (tenant × meter × api_key × period) cartesian, which is the exact shape Stripe / Lago / OpenMeter / Orb optimise their hot path for.
technical_fit.typical_state_lifecycle_and_ttl: 12+ months at a minimum for invoice replay (most SaaS contracts allow a 90-day dispute window plus a 12-month reconciliation horizon). 7 years is the practical floor for SOX/SOC1 buyers retaining accounts-payable / accounts-receivable records on the cold tier — but only the closed-period aggregates and the raw event log need to live for 7 years; the hot per-(tenant, meter, current-period) counter only needs to live for the current period + a grace window of 7–30 days for late-arriving events, after which it rolls into a cold immutable audit store. Hot state lifecycle in a feature-server tier is therefore 30–60 days; cold archive is years. This is the single biggest architectural mismatch with beava-as-it-stands: beava is in-memory only and its WAL+snapshot is a hot-state durability story, not a 7-year audit-archive story.
technical_fit.typical_feature_count_per_decision: 1–5 features per inline quota / credit gate (credit_balance_remaining, usage_total_current_period, plan_quota_remaining, velocity_1m, kill_switch_active) — batch_get in one round-trip. 10–50 features per customer-portal dashboard refresh (per-meter usage_total + trend + projected_invoice_amount). 100–10k features per invoice close (every (tenant, meter, billing_period) tuple for the closing period).
technical_fit.durability_requirements: Regulator-grade — this is the single most durability-sensitive domain in the entire use-case list. Losing 5 minutes of counter increments in a node restart is unacceptable because every lost increment is lost revenue and every double-counted increment is a customer dispute / regulator-visible defect. The standard pattern is: durable WAL on the raw event log + idempotent transactional commits to the aggregator + periodic snapshot + cold archive of the closed event log to S3/Parquet/object-storage with object-lock for SOX. beava's WAL + periodic snapshot story covers the hot tier; what's missing relative to Lago/OpenMeter is (a) the raw event log as a first-class durable artefact survives independently of beava's snapshot, (b) cold-archive sink to S3/Parquet, (c) cross-region replication, (d) tested replay-from-WAL after node loss with idempotency guarantees that match the producer's idempotency_key contract. The 'refuse-on-network-FS' restriction is fine — Stripe / Metronome / Lago all co-locate hot state with the process anyway — but the in-memory-only constraint means the cold archive must live somewhere else.
technical_fit.deployment_topology_fit: Single-binary regional fits well for the inline quota-gate role (one beava per region beside the API gateway / LLM router, doing sub-ms reads and writes locally). Multi-region active-active is harder than for observability because the credit-balance counter is a strong-consistency requirement: if two regions both think there is 1 credit left and both serve a 1-credit request, the invoice is wrong. The industry workaround is to (a) shard by tenant_id so each tenant pins to one region, or (b) accept eventual consistency with a small safety margin (well-known in Stripe / Cloudflare Durable Object rate-limit literature). beava v0 has no in-process sharding, so for very large platforms (>684k EPS or >50 GB hot state per region) buyers must hand-shard externally — the same gap that constrains the observability use case but with a sharper financial cost when it fails.

commercial_fit.who_buys: Primary buyer is the billing-platform / monetisation-platform engineering team that sits between Product and Finance — the same team that today is choosing between Stripe Billing Meter, Metronome (now Stripe), Orb, Lago, OpenMeter, Chargebee, Recurly, Zuora, and Microsoft's Metered Billing Accelerator. Secondary buyers are (a) Platform-Engineering teams at AI / LLM-API companies who already built a homegrown token-meter on Redis or Kafka and now need to add audit-grade durability and reconcilable invoices, (b) Developer-platform / API-as-a-product teams (Twilio, SendGrid, Algolia, Pinecone-style businesses) who need per-API-key real-time quota enforcement plus monthly invoice computation, (c) FinOps teams at enterprise SaaS who need chargeback to internal cost centres at a sub-org grain. Finance / billing-ops is the budget owner and the audit-control owner; engineering builds and runs the pipe.
commercial_fit.market_size_signal: Very strong signal: Stripe acquired Metronome for roughly $1B in January 2026, citing 'metered pricing is the native business model for the AI era' — the highest-signal datapoint in the entire use-case ladder. PitchBook profiles list Metronome's pre-acquisition valuation in the high-hundred-millions; Orb has raised at >$1B valuation; Lago is an open-core OSS challenger with public ClickHouse-Cloud collaboration. Independent analyst estimates put the broader recurring-and-cloud-billing-software market at ~$6–7B in 2024–2025 with forecasts of $13–15B+ by the early 2030s. 67–77% of SaaS companies now use some form of consumption-based pricing (up from ~52% in 2022). The slice beava can serve — the metering pipe itself, not the full billing/invoicing/AR suite — is the most defensible sub-segment because it is the high-throughput, low-latency, exactly-once layer that every billing vendor has had to (re)build. [uncertain]
commercial_fit.urgency_drivers: 1) The shift from seat-based SaaS to usage-based / AI-native pricing has already happened — Stripe-Metronome at $1B in January 2026 is the public watermark, and every AI platform that bills per token (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, hundreds of agentic startups) needs a real-time token-meter that is reconcilable to the cent. 2) Stripe Billing Meter Events v2 publicly caps at 10k req/s livemode by default — companies beyond that scale are explicitly told to 'contact sales' or build upstream, which is exactly the wedge Metronome / Lago / OpenMeter occupy and where a feature-server-style upstream pre-aggregator can land. 3) AI cost-control: per-tenant token-velocity counters for runaway-agent / leaked-key / abuse detection are now a top-3 ask for any team running LLM endpoints in production, and Datadog / Prometheus / a warehouse can't serve them in <5 ms. 4) Audit / SOX / SOC1: as usage-based SaaS becomes more common, the finance org's appetite for 'we hope the count is right' shrinks — explicit two-stream reconciliation (live counter + raw event log replay) is becoming table stakes. 5) Open-core fatigue: Lago and OpenMeter are Apache-2.0 OSS challengers to commercial incumbents and have visible community pull (Lago: tens of thousands of GitHub stars and a public ClickHouse-Cloud case study; OpenMeter: YC-backed, Apache-2.0, used by AI platforms).
commercial_fit.regulatory_or_audit_constraints: SOX (revenue-recognition controls on usage-based revenue lines) is the dominant constraint for any public-company billing pipeline; the practical control is ITGC + 'two aggregations must tie' reconciliation, with 7-year retention on the underlying record per US PCAOB guidance. SOC 1 (financial-controls audit) is table-stakes for any billing vendor selling into mid-market and up. SOC 2 type II is table-stakes for any SaaS holding tenant-level metadata at all. PCI-DSS scope creeps in only if the meter pipeline touches card data (it generally should not — Stripe Billing isolates this). GDPR / CCPA matter because customer_id / api_key_id / occasionally end-user-id are processed; right-to-erasure interacts awkwardly with 7-year financial retention (the standard resolution is to retain pseudonymised aggregates and erase the PII map). AML matters only for the subset of buyers who are themselves money-movers (crypto exchanges, fintechs) — for them the metering pipe doubles as part of the txn-monitoring evidence chain. The combined effect is that this domain has the strictest durability + retention + audit requirement of any use case in the beava ladder.
commercial_fit.time_to_value_signal: 1–3 days to a working 'per-(tenant, api_key, meter_name, billing_period) SUM + COUNT + projected_invoice_amount' demo on a laptop using @bv.event for meter_event and @bv.table for the aggregations, fed by an HTTP-push shim from the application code. 2–6 weeks to a production pilot in the inline-quota-gate role for an AI / API-as-a-product business that already has its own invoice-rating pipeline (the buyer plugs beava in front of Lago / Stripe and uses it for the <5 ms gate). 6+ months to a credible source-of-truth invoicing role, because the durability / cold-archive / audit-replay story has to be built out (today this is a non-starter on beava v0 alone — see open_engineering_gaps).

competition.incumbents: Commercial usage-based-billing platforms: Stripe Billing Meter Events / Meter Event Streams v2 (post-Metronome-acquisition, January 2026), Metronome (now part of Stripe), Orb (250k+ EPS, SQL-over-raw-events, ClickHouse-backed), Chargebee, Recurly, Zuora, Maxio (SaaSOptics + Chargify merger), Togai, Schematic, Flexprice, Solvimon, Sequence. Open-source: Lago (Apache-2.0, ClickHouse + Kafka, 1M EPS demonstrated, tens of thousands of GitHub stars), OpenMeter (Apache-2.0, YC-backed, ClickHouse + Kafka + CloudEvents), Microsoft Metered Billing Accelerator (.NET + EventHub). DIY stacks: Kafka + ClickHouse + a thin aggregator (the Lago / Metronome / OpenMeter pattern), Kafka + Flink + Postgres / DynamoDB, Redis + Lua + a periodic flush to S3 (the Twilio-style historical pattern), Cloudflare Workers + Durable Objects + Analytics Engine (Cloudflare's own metering stack). Storage primitives competitors: Redis (for the hot quota counter, with Lua-atomic increment), Cloudflare Durable Objects (the per-customer-singleton pattern, eventually-consistent but globally addressable), Aerospike, ScyllaDB.
competition.competitive_incumbent_per_domain: For the metering-pipe-specifically slice (ingest + dedupe + aggregate + serve, separate from invoicing / AR / dunning): Stripe Billing Meter is the public default at small/medium scale (≤10k EPS in livemode); Metronome / Orb / Lago / OpenMeter are the named alternatives once you exceed that bar or need pricing flexibility Stripe doesn't offer (SQL-over-raw-events, replay, multidimensional rating, prepaid wallets). Lago publicly demonstrates 1M EPS on ClickHouse Cloud and is the dominant Apache-2.0 OSS choice. OpenMeter is the closest architectural cousin to where beava might sit (CloudEvents ingest, real-time aggregation, Apache-2.0). For the inline-quota-gate slice specifically: Redis-Lua (industry default), Cloudflare Durable Objects (the globally-coordinated singleton variant), Envoy global ratelimit (Lyft ratelimit service, Redis-backed) — beava's pitch here is sub-ms TCP+msgpack vs Redis-Lua's ~1–5 ms, plus first-class velocity / tier-bracket primitives that today are hand-rolled in Lua.
competition.beava_differentiator: 1) Sub-ms TCP+msgpack get / batch_get is fast enough that beava can serve the inline-quota-gate AND the metering pipe from one tier — Lago / OpenMeter / Orb cannot (their ClickHouse query latency is 50–500 ms, fine for invoicing, too slow for the gate). 2) 50+ aggregation primitives mean tiered / graduated / velocity / max-concurrent rating is a declarative @bv.table, not a hand-rolled Lua-on-Redis script or a per-customer SQL recording rule. 3) No Kafka / no Flink / no ClickHouse / no Redis-cluster dependency — single binary deploys behind the API gateway or beside the LLM router, attractive for mid-market platforms who don't want to operate the Lago/OpenMeter stack. 4) Apache-2.0 no-open-core — same posture as Lago and OpenMeter, more permissive than Stripe-Metronome commercial. 5) Push-on-event over HTTP/JSON :8080 or TCP+msgpack :8081 is a natural fit for application-code direct push, and msgpack throughput beats the JSON-over-HTTPS path that Stripe Meter Event Streams v2 uses. 6) Velocity / recency primitives are first-class — beava can express 'rate-of-change of token consumption for tenant X in last 30 s' as a feature read, which today is either a Redis-Lua hand-roll or a ClickHouse SQL window function (and the latter is too slow for inline use).
competition.where_beava_loses_today: 1) Durability story is hot-state-only — beava's WAL + periodic snapshot is enough for restart survival but NOT enough for 'reconstruct December's invoice in March from the durable raw event log'. The buyer needs a durable raw-event log that survives independently of beava's snapshot, with cold archive to S3/Parquet/object-lock for SOX. This is a hard gap and the single biggest reason beava cannot be the source-of-truth metering today. 2) No TLS, no auth in v0 — disqualifying for any production deployment that ingests cross-tenant data (which is all of them). 3) No in-process sharding — a single very-large platform (>684k EPS or hundreds of GB hot state across api_key cardinality) must hand-shard externally, whereas Lago / Metronome / Stripe shard internally. 4) No idempotency-by-event-id at the wire level — producers need to assert exactly-once via an idempotency_key contract (Stripe pattern, OpenMeter pattern); beava v0 does not document a corresponding native idempotency-key dedup primitive. 5) No raw-event archive / replay — fundamental to audit reconciliation; Lago/OpenMeter/Stripe all keep raw events durably and let you re-aggregate at any time. 6) No multidimensional rating engine — Orb's SQL-over-raw-events and Stripe-Metronome's product catalog with thousands of rates are out of scope for beava (it serves counters, it does not compute invoices). This is fine if beava is positioned as the upstream pre-aggregator, not as the billing system. 7) No cross-region active-active for strong-consistency credit-balance — the well-known correctness corner-case of the prepaid-wallet pattern. 8) No documented case study or reference customer in this domain. [uncertain]
competition.integration_surface: Producers: direct application-code push over HTTP/JSON or TCP+msgpack (the natural front door — Stripe, OpenMeter, Lago all accept this); Kafka consumer (would be a strong adoption lever for the existing Lago/OpenMeter/Metronome architectural cohort — does not exist in beava v0); AWS Marketplace metering API hand-off; an LLM-gateway sidecar (LiteLLM, OpenRouter, Kong AI Gateway) emitting a meter event per request — the LiteLLM Lago integration GitHub issue thread (#5477, #8243) shows real demand. Consumers: inline quota / credit gates (Envoy ext_authz, Kong custom plugin, an LLM-gateway pre-call hook, Cloudflare Worker), invoice computation jobs (Lago / Stripe / a homegrown rater) reading closed-period aggregates via batch_get, customer-facing 'current usage' UI panels (sub-second read), FinOps cost-attribution dashboards (read-heavy, latency-tolerant).
competition.scoring_engine_coupling: Mostly an external rules / rating engine (Stripe Billing, Lago, Orb, Metronome — each owns the price catalog and the invoice computation) reading beava counters via batch_get for the invoice. The inline-quota-gate decision is sometimes pure-counter ('credit_balance_remaining > cost ? allow : deny') and sometimes wraps an external policy engine (OPA, Cedar, in-house) for plan-tier rules. No ML scorer involvement; this is the most deterministic / least-ML domain in the use-case ladder.

[uncertain] Comparable production references at incumbents and adjacent products: Lago has public ClickHouse-Cloud case study describing scale from 10k EPS to 1M EPS to serve a single named enterprise; OpenMeter is YC-backed (Apache-2.0) and publicly describes its Kafka + ClickHouse + custom-Go-consumer architecture with exactly-once dedup by (event_id, source) for 32 days; Stripe Billing Meter Event Streams v2 publishes 10k req/s livemode default rate-limit; Orb publishes 250k+ EPS and a SQL-over-raw-events architecture; Microsoft Metered Billing Accelerator is a public Apache-2.0 reference for AWS-Marketplace-style metering. Stripe's $1B acquisition of Metronome in January 2026 is the highest-signal commercial datapoint in the entire use-case ladder. LiteLLM's open GitHub issues (#5477, #8243) for Lago integration show the AI-gateway-→-metering integration pattern is in active demand. Cloudflare publishes its own Durable-Objects-+-Analytics-Engine pattern for per-customer rate limiting + metering. None of these is a beava reference; they validate the market and shape.
adoption_signals.community_discussions: No beava-specific Discord / GitHub Discussion threads located on this topic. [uncertain] Broader community signal is exceptionally strong: Lago GitHub Issues + Wiki (tens of thousands of stars), OpenMeter GitHub (YC-backed Apache-2.0 with documented metering challenges), LiteLLM GitHub Issues for token-meter integrations, Stripe Metered Billing 2026 guides on Dev.to and engineering blogs, the WarpStream 'Anatomy of a serverless usage-based billing system' write-up, public Hacker News threads on Stripe-Metronome acquisition, r/SaaS / r/aws threads on Stripe-Billing-rate-limit pain, OpenMeter's 'Usage Deduplication is Challenging' and 'The Metering Challenge' blog posts.
adoption_signals.examples_or_demos_in_repo: No dedicated billing / metering / SaaS-quota demo identified in the repository. The python/beava/demos/ directory contains adtech, ecommerce and fraud subtrees but no billing / metering / saas-quota subtree at the time of review. A purpose-built demo (meter_event → per-(tenant, api_key, meter_name, billing_period) SUM + COUNT + tiered_bracket_index + projected_invoice_amount + credit_balance_remaining, served via batch_get for an inline LLM-gateway quota gate and via a /usage HTTP endpoint for the customer portal) would be a strong differentiator vs. Lago / OpenMeter / Stripe and would lean directly into the Stripe-Metronome-acquisition narrative. [uncertain]
adoption_signals.adversarial_pressure_level: Moderate — meaningfully more adversarial than observability but less than fraud / AML. Adversaries actively try to (a) leak / share API keys to circumvent per-key quotas, (b) script burst patterns to overshoot a credit balance before the gate refreshes, (c) game tiered pricing (split usage across many small tenants to stay in the cheap bracket), (d) replay-attack meter-event emit endpoints to inflate or deflate counters. The exactly-once / idempotency-key contract is partly an adversary-mitigation as well as a reliability mitigation. Drift is moderate (plan tiers change quarterly, new meters launch a few times per year, model prices change frequently in the AI segment).

risk_and_non_goals.non_goals: 1) Being the system-of-record source-of-truth invoice generator — beava v0 is the upstream metering pipe, not the rating / catalog / invoice / AR / dunning / revenue-recognition stack. Lago / Stripe Billing / Metronome / Orb / Chargebee / Zuora own this layer and beava is not trying to compete with them. 2) 7-year cold archive — beava is in-memory only; the durable raw event log and the closed-period audit archive must live in S3 / Parquet / a TSDB / a warehouse alongside, not inside beava. 3) Multidimensional rating with thousands of prices — that is Metronome / Orb territory; beava serves the aggregated quantities, the rating engine multiplies them by price. 4) Cross-entity joins (this customer's usage joined to their parent org's commit-tier joined to their FX rate) — that is warehouse work; beava only serves per-key features. 5) Tax computation, dunning, payment retries, revenue recognition (ASC 606 / IFRS 15) — explicit non-goals; these are the rest of the billing stack. 6) Long historical analytics ('show me this customer's usage trend over the last 18 months') — that is warehouse / TSDB work; beava's hot window is 30–60 days max.
risk_and_non_goals.open_engineering_gaps: Concrete features beava would need to ship to be production-grade for this domain, roughly in priority order: 1) Durable raw-event log as a first-class artifact, independent of beava's snapshot, with the same idempotency-key contract producers expect (Stripe-pattern UUID-unique-within-24h); without this, beava cannot satisfy 'replay the raw events in March to reconstruct December's closed invoice' which is the table-stakes audit control. 2) Native idempotency-key dedup primitive on the ingest path — every meter_event has a producer-assigned UUID, beava must reject duplicates within a configurable window (24 h default per Stripe convention, 32 d per OpenMeter convention) and surface dedup-rejection metrics. 3) TLS termination + auth model (token / mTLS / OIDC) on :8080, :8081, :8090 — without these, no production billing deployment is possible outside a strictly trusted VPC, which rules out cross-team / cross-tenant work. 4) Cold-archive sink to S3 / Parquet / object-lock (SOX-grade) plus a documented retention / archival lifecycle — every billing tier above ships this. 5) Native EXACT-not-approximate guarantee on the billing-primary counters and explicit fencing of HLL / CMS / t-digest to non-billing overlays — finance auditors will not accept probabilistic dollar amounts. 6) Tumbling-calendar-month window primitive with late-arriving-event handling (slot into correct period by occurred_at, not arrival time, with a documented grace-cutoff) — Lago has this and beava needs it. 7) Tiered / graduated / volume-bracket rating as first-class declarative @bv.table primitives so 'current_bracket_index' and 'projected_invoice_amount' are feature reads, not bespoke application code. 8) Triggers / 'fire when credit_balance crosses 50% / 80% / 95% / 100%' for usage-alert / kill-switch workflows — the canonical credit-wallet UX. 9) Per-tenant write-quotas / per-tenant rate-limit accounting on beava's own ingress (the multi-tenancy story so a beava operator can rate-limit their own customers, the same shape Mimir's tenant-limits subsystem provides). 10) In-process or sidecar sharding by tenant_id prefix for very large platforms (>684k EPS or >50 GB hot state per region). 11) A Kafka consumer entrypoint to drop into the existing Lago / OpenMeter / Metronome architectural cohort transparently. 12) Documented exactly-once-from-Kafka semantics including consumer-offset commit + idempotent aggregator (the OpenMeter playbook). 13) An OpenTelemetry-CloudEvents producer surface so the existing OTel / CloudEvents producer cohort can target beava without a custom SDK. 14) Cross-region replication for the credit-balance counter with a documented consistency model (or an explicit 'shard by tenant; tenant is region-pinned' guidance).
risk_and_non_goals.trigger_action_required: Yes — strongly preferred. The credit-wallet UX (alert at 50/80/95%, hard-stop at 100%) and the runaway-script / leaked-key kill-switch both naturally express as 'fire when usage_total or velocity crosses threshold' triggers. Polling every key every few seconds across millions of (tenant, api_key, meter) tuples is wasteful and slower than a callback. Pure invoice-computation paths only need feature serving, not triggers (the rater pulls closed-period aggregates on a schedule).
